narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Boots That Talked
This is Gumboot dance. late 19th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (fYYYymWvhAI)
Title card: Gumboot dance · South Africa · late 19th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in the late 19th century among black miners in South Africa.
It served as a secret communication system to bypass bans on speaking.
Over time, it incorporated traditional rural dances and evolved into a form of social expression and satire against mine authorities.
on_screen: Map: South Africa · Africa
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically used for communication and as a morale booster, it is now a performance art.
It serves as a cultural record of the miners' struggle, resistance, and identity, often performed at festivals and in public plazas.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Aman Folk Ensemble presents The Immigrants (https://archive.org/details/calauem_000460)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers wear Wellington boots, often adorned with bells or bottle caps to create percussive sounds.
The movement involves rhythmic stamping, slapping the boots with hands, and total body articulation.
It is a percussive, polyrhythmic dance that parodies the movements of mine guards.
Watch for Boot Slap, Stomp.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (fYYYymWvhAI)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Group formations in streets or plazas.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Originally performed without instruments, the dance relies on the body and boots as idiophones.
Modern accompaniments often include guitar, accordion, and violin, particularly in the style of township jive (mbaqanga).
Listen for the Body (idiophone), Wellington boots, Bells, Bottle caps.
A percussive soundscape dominated by the rhythmic stamping of boots and the metallic rattling of bells or bottle caps, often accompanied by guitar-led township jive.

Costumes vary by group, ranging from work-related gear like helmets to school uniforms or traditional attire.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The Rishile Gumboot Dancers of Soweto, directed by Zenzi Mbuli, are a prominent group.
The Black Umfolosi folk group from Zimbabwe is also noted for their performances.
Variants exist across South Africa, with local groups adapting the dance to reflect their specific cultural backgrounds and modern circumstances.
The dance shares stylistic similarities with African-American 'stepping' and is rooted in the traditional dances of the rural areas from which the miners originated.
